newsitem.title: USA: Nader seeks changes in Kaiser Permante's HMO care.
newsitem.headline: Nader seeks changes in Kaiser Permante's HMO care.

text.p: Consumer advocate Ralph Nader on Tuesday said Kaiser Permante, the largest U.S. health maintenance organization, should be barred from enrolling new members until it corrects practices that he said pose "a direct threat" to the safety of its patients.

In a letter to the California Department of Corporations, Nader said deficiencies in emergency care at Kaiser were "systemic" throughout its network and have led to a series of "medical malpractice tragedies."

Nader cited Kaiser's plans to reduce the numbers of nurses on its staff and internal Kaiser documents detailing other cost-savings initiatives he said were degrading the quality of care. He also called attention to a series of wrongful death lawsuits filed against the health-care provider.

Last week, regulators in Texas responded to some of the patient lawsuits against Kaiser by slapping it with a $1 million fine and ordering it to implement specific steps to improve the quality of its care.
Nader said it was time for regulators in California, where most of Kaiser's operations are based, to take similar steps.
Kaiser was not immediately available to comment on Nader's letter, which the consumer advocate made public. But the company has in the past defended its practices.

Kaiser says that while the size of its nursing staff has been cut, the reduction corresponds to a drop in the average length of hospital stays. It also claims that shorten hospital stays are often made possible by improvements in medical technology and not dictated by budgetary concerns.

Still, the HMO is increasingly finding itself at the center of the attack on the managed care industry. A Kaiser facility in Los Angeles was one of the first hospitals in the nation to come under attack in 1995 for discharging newborns as early as eight hours after delivery. More recently, it has been criticized for a business plan that rations high-cost drugs and limits emergency room admissions.
